Photograph: Ezra Acayan/Getty Images Nepal-Tibet flood disaster Nepal-Tibet deaths from flash flooding rise amid race to free workers in tunnel Total of confirmed 797 dead and more than 3,000 missing amid threat of fresh inundation Nepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updates ‘Their whole village has disappeared’: frantic hunt for survivors in Kathmandu hospital Angelique Chrisafis and agencies Sun 30 Aug 2026 11.43 EDT First published on Sat 29 Aug 2026 23.39 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Rescuers in Nepal and Tibet have battled through leg-sucking mud amid the threat of fresh flooding to search for thousands of people still missing after a deadly wall of water swept through the Himalayan border zone, engulfing entire villages. The latest updates on Sunday put the number of missing at 3,048, including hundreds of foreigners. There was a total of 797 confirmed deaths across Nepal and Tibet, and reports of some bodies swept downstream possibly as far as India. Nepal said it had begun the task of burying some of the hundreds of bodies after first taking DNA samples so that families could later reclaim them after identification and perform traditional funeral rites. The disaster, which struck the border on Wednesday morning, was caused by a glacial collapse which sent a wall of water and debris downstream, the US Geological Survey said. Nepal’s foreign minister called for a global response to the climate crisis, saying the small, poor Himalayan nation was bearing a disproportionate share of its impact. “Despite having only 0.1% contribution to global emissions, people of Nepal have become major victims of climate change,” Shisir Khanal said on Saturday. View image in fullscreen A vehicle drives past houses covered in mud in Baireni, in the Dhading district of Nepal. Photograph: Manan Vatsyayana/AFP/Getty Images More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far. Nepal said on Sunday that 2,502 people, including 592 foreigners, were out of contact in the country. It reported an updated death toll of 781 people. Chinese authorities on Sunday reported 16 deaths and 546 missing, of whom 261 were foreign nationals, including 104 from Nepal, 49 from India, 33 from Latvia, 18 from the US and 15 British citizens. In a breakthrough at the weekend, Nepal’s army was able to insert a pipe into a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydroelectric site, where more than 100 workers are believed to be trapped. The home minister, Sudan Gurung, said: “We have already started sending air through the small opening, and we will now begin excavation work and send the rescue team inside.” It is a race to reach the workers, who may still be alive inside the tunnels, with rescue efforts focused on the Trishuli 3A and 3B sites. They are among 933 hydropower workers who are among the missing, according to Nepal’s disaster authority. View image in fullscreen Soldiers search for bodies as rescue operations shift into search and retrieval in Nepal. Photograph: Ezra Acayan/Getty Images Nepal warned on Sunday of rising flood waters and urged rescue teams to exercise caution. “We have received information that the flood flow in the Bhotekoshi river in Rasuwa has increased further,” the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said. Flood warnings were sent to people’s phones early on Sunday as rescue crews worked to clear a highway connecting Kathmandu to one of the areas hit by the floods. ‘The flood took everything I have’: survivors grieve for relatives and homes swept away in Nepal Read more In Dhading, one of the worst-hit regions in Nepal, some people began returning to ruined homes to see what could be salvaged. Residents of the flood-hit villages said they were struggling to make sense of near-constant alarms they had received since the initial floods. One resident, Govind Shreshta, told the Associated Press: “Sometimes they say a flood is coming, then we have to run again to higher ground, even at night. There is also rain. It’s really difficult for me. I have a 72-year-old father and 70-year-old mum. I must carry them and I am exhausted. It’s going on like this for those who are still alive.” 2:04 ‘I have lost everything’: survivors reflect after deadly flood in Nepal – video The government estimated Nepal’s reconstruction bill could run to billions of dollars. Officials in Nepal called for forensic testing kits to identify bodies and freezer units to store them in, saying bodies that had been in water could decompose at a faster rate. Survivors face an agonising wait to learn the fate of missing relatives and the prospect of rebuilding their lives from nothing. “All the settlements near the river were swept away,” Buddhi Ram Dangol told Agence France-Presse in Nepal’s Nuwakot district. “There is nothing left.” View image in fullscreen Firefighters conduct search and rescue operations along a river in Gyirong county in Tibet. Photograph: cnsphoto/Reuters In Tibet, where Chinese authorities are the only source of information, rescue operations were paused at the hardest-hit area of Gyirong over the risk of more flooding from a newly formed lake. A total of 2,141 rescuers were near the Gyirong site, the Xinhua state news agency reported, including more than 500 in the worst-hit area. In Kathmandu, Nepal’s capital, relatives and friends gathered outside the main government hospital from early morning, desperately searching for news of missing loved ones. Many shuffled between the help desk and the hospital noticeboard, clutching photographs and scanning lists of patients in the hope of finding them. Dil Maya Lama stood weeping near the help desk at the hospital, searching for information about her 26-year-old brother, a driver for a hydropower company in Rasuwa. She had travelled from Ramechhap, about 80 miles (130km) away. “I came here with the hope that I might find him,” she told the Associated Press. “There is no information about him.” Nelza Moktan sought information about her missing cousin, who also worked as a driver in Rasuwa. “I feel hopeless. It has already been four days,” she said. Kalinskas / BNS Lithuaniaâs Interior Ministry is proposing to restore police and other law enforcement officersâ ability to fire warning shots and ease some restrictions on when they can use their firearms, saying the changes would strengthen officersâ protection. The proposals have drawn scepticism from police unions, which say they were not consulted during their preparation and question whether warning shots should be brought back. Under current rules, an officer may use a firearm when there is an unavoidable danger and an unavoidable necessity. The Interior Ministry wants to remove those specific requirements. Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas said the current wording relies too heavily on subjective assessments, which can be difficult for an officer to make in a rapidly developing situation. âThese are statements of an evaluative nature. If the state asks an officer to do their job and the officer has 1 to 10 seconds to make a decision, can they assess whether there is an unavoidable danger?â Katelynas said. Martynas Katelynas | J. StaceviÄius / LRT He stressed that firearms would remain a last resort under the proposed rules. âThe firearm is used in a way that causes as little harm as possible, while the safeguards are being further strengthened,â said Darius Domarkas, head of the ministryâs Public Security Group. The ministry also wants to restore the option of firing a warning shot into the air as an additional means of de-escalating a situation. âThere was no possibility of firing a warning shot into the air as an additional warning when a situation is escalating and needs to be de-escalated,â Domarkas said. âThere was only a verbal warning.â Warning shots were abolished in Lithuania about a decade ago. Former police officer and instructor Dalius Mackela said there were good reasons for removing them. âIf we fire those 9 grams into the air, they don't just disappear,â Mackela said, referring to the approximate weight of a bullet. âIf, God forbid, that 9-gram bullet comes back down and finds an object, someone will be hurt. Who will stand up for the officers then?â Border guard (associative image) | V. Raupelis / LRT Mackela also questioned whether the proposed changes were necessary, saying existing legislation already clearly establishes when police may use firearms. The debate over firearms use intensified this summer after a group of irregular migrants attacked border guards. Under the ministryâs proposals, border guards would have more flexibility to use firearms against equipment used to cross the border. âThey could act against equipment used for illegal border crossings, such as ladders or tunnels,â Katelynas said. The minister also said officers who fire at a suspect would be guaranteed legal and psychological assistance. Police unions, however, say changes to firearms rules alone would not address their concerns. âThe whole complicated situation is being turned into a show, with the emphasis being placed where it shouldnât be,â said Ineta KurseviÄienÄ, head of the Federation of Police Trade Unions. Roma KatinienÄ, chairwoman of the Police Trade Union, said law enforcement agencies needed an agreement on procedures following the use of firearms or special measures. âWhat is needed is a common agreement among law enforcement institutions on simplified procedures when a firearm or special measures are used, so that officers do not become hostages to three or five years of litigation,â KatinienÄ said. The unions pointed to several lengthy cases involving officers. In May, a court acquitted police officer Darius Å erpytis, who had been charged with causing a death by exceeding his powers. The investigation and court proceedings lasted three years. A separate case involving border guard Karolis IlgeviÄius has been ongoing for two years. He is accused of shooting at the tire of a fleeing suspected smugglerâs vehicle and killing the driver. The unions also criticised the Interior Ministry for failing to consult them before preparing the proposed changes. âUnfortunately, with the current interior minister, as a trade union, we have not had a single meeting,â the Police Trade Union chairwoman said. Katelynas said the unions would now have an opportunity to give their views on the proposals. He said Lithuaniaâs security environment had changed and that law enforcement officers therefore needed rules adapted to the new circumstances. LRT English Newsletter Every Friday morning.
